nameStory: The species name 'formica' comes from the Latin word for ant, suggesting this tiny spider may resemble an ant in some way or perhaps mimics ant behavior. Like many small spiders, it may have earned this name by scurrying about in an ant-like manner when disturbed.
description: Scotinella formica is a tiny member of the guardstone spider family, one of the less familiar spider groups in New England. These are small, ground-dwelling spiders that don't build the typical webs we associate with most spiders. Instead, they hunt actively for prey among leaf litter and low vegetation. With only two confirmed sightings in New England, this is truly a rare find for any spider enthusiast.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, likely only a few millimeters in body length - about the size of a small ant or smaller

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web construction - this is a hunting spider that actively pursues prey on the ground

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Fast-moving and ant-like in its scurrying movements when disturbed, quickly darting for cover

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, robust build typical of ground-hunting spiders with relatively short legs for its body size

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found at ground level among leaf litter, under stones, or in low vegetation where it can hunt small prey

habitat: This extremely rare spider likely inhabits leaf litter, under stones, or among low vegetation in forested areas. Given its scarcity in New England records, it may prefer specific microhabitats that haven't been thoroughly surveyed. Look in undisturbed woodland floors with rich organic matter.

seasonality.spring: May become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots to begin hunting. Most likely to be spotted during this active period.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be encountered. This is the best time to search for this elusive species.
seasonality.fall: Activity may continue into early fall before seeking overwintering sites. Late season searches might still yield sightings.
seasonality.winter: Inactive, likely hidden under deep leaf litter, logs, or stones in a dormant state until spring warmth returns.

funFact: With only two recorded sightings in all of New England, finding a Scotinella formica would be like discovering a spider unicorn - you'd be among fewer than a handful of people to have encountered this species in the region!
confusionNotes: Due to its tiny size and ant-like behavior, it could easily be mistaken for an actual ant at first glance. Look carefully for the spider's two body segments (versus an ant's three) and eight legs instead of six.
contextualKnowledge: The family name Phrurolithidae means 'guardstone spiders,' though the origin of this common name isn't entirely clear. These spiders were once classified in different families, which is why you might see the old scientific name Phruronellus formica in older references.
compareHints: Scotinella formica can be distinguished from its relative Scotinella pallida primarily through careful examination by experts, as the differences are quite subtle. Both are extremely small ground-dwelling hunters, but pallida (meaning 'pale') may have lighter coloration. Given the rarity of both species, any tiny hunting spider in leaf litter deserves close photographic documentation.
